metaData.originalTitle: The U.S. signed up for the 2026 FIFA World Cup – and its 11 host cities are paying for it
metaData.title: The U.S. signed up for the 2026 FIFA World Cup – and its 11 host cities are paying for it
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This investigation reveals the immense financial burden and contractual frustrations U.S. host cities face for the 2026 World Cup, as FIFA retains nearly all revenue while cities pay billions in costs, leading to a push for better terms for the 2031 Women's World Cup.
metaData.summary: This in-depth investigation by The Athletic examines the financial dynamics between FIFA and the 11 U.S. host cities for the 2026 men's World Cup. It details how FIFA's hosting agreements require cities to cover massive costs—including transportation, security, stadium upgrades, and fan fest operations—while FIFA retains the vast majority of revenue from ticketing, media rights, and sponsorship. The article highlights specific examples of these costs, such as a $25.8 million jail in Kansas City, $57.8 million in waived tax revenue, and a $15 million broadcast center in Dallas that will be demolished. It also reveals a letter signed by 21 U.S. cities, including 7 of the 2026 host cities, warning U.S. Soccer that they will not accept similar terms for the 2031 Women's World Cup without meaningful negotiation on cost-sharing, revenue participation, and expense caps. The piece captures the growing exasperation of city officials, from the infamous 'put your city on the map' comment to the scaled-back fan fest plans and the push for a more equitable partnership in the future.

mainPoints.point: FIFA's hosting agreements place the vast majority of financial burdens on host cities while FIFA retains nearly all revenue.
mainPoints.explanation: Cities are responsible for costs related to transportation, security, stadium upgrades, and fan fests, while FIFA keeps revenue from ticketing, media rights, and sponsorships.

mainPoints.point: U.S. host cities are deeply frustrated with the one-sided financial terms and lack of transparency.
mainPoints.explanation: The article documents numerous examples of frustration, including a FIFA executive telling LA officials the tournament would 'put your city on the map,' and cities struggling with unexpected costs like 'clean stadium' requirements and police escorts for VIPs.

mainPoints.point: Cities are leveraging their experience to demand better terms for the 2031 Women's World Cup bid.
mainPoints.explanation: A letter signed by 21 cities, including 7 of the 2026 host cities, warns U.S. Soccer that they will not accept similar terms without meaningful negotiation on cost-sharing, revenue participation, and expense caps.
